EDIT: I'm basing this off something I posted in /r/ukpolitics so it's written largely from a UK perspective!

This idea would actually be quite similar in concept to the EU as it is currently headed except instead of a shambles of vastly different cultures, histories and economies I propose a Union of countries that share a common language, have cultural similarities and ultimately a common origin. Such a Union would have a much simpler structure than the EU, it would not be aimed at creating a superstate but it would absorb some of the functions of the member states in order to ensure economic stability. It would be organised along currently existing lines, America, the UK (and potentially Ireland if they chose), Australia, Canada and New Zealand would represent the first layer with the constituent states representing the second. As all but the UK are federal countries already this would work elegantly and would present us with the perfect opportunity to instate long-needed constitutional reform in the UK.

This Union would be inspired by the EU but recognise and learn from it's flaws. It would implement free movement of labour, free trade and a common citizenship in addition to national citizenship. However, instead of a union aimed at eventually eliminating the nations in favour of a superstate this union would be aimed at preserving and empowering it's member nations, working together for common prosperity where it is practical and leaving everything else alone. Obviously there must be a small amount of political integration for such a project to work but instead of the gradual but total approach of the EU this Union would absorb powers only when vital for the function of the common market. Instead of the nations working for the Union the Union would work for the nations. The common citizenship would not replace the national citizenship but enhance it, allowing military and diplomatic co-operation on an unprecedented scale. There would be no attempt at a single currency as this undermines national sovereignty and no directive would be passed without the consent of all the nations.

Instead of a sprawling mass of semi-democratic bodies this Union would have just two major ones: an elected House of Nations and a technocratic Senate. The House of Nations would consist of Members elected by constituent state rather than by country, this makes it nearly impossible for say England to take all the UK seats to prevent Scotland from having a voice. It also makes it harder for one country to dominate the others. The number of seats would be based on population and re-assessed every decade. The Senate would be technocratic, again membership would be state-based and proportional to population. Members would be appointed based on their expertise, for example a First Lord/Senator (it could use either British or US titles, the names are of little concern) of Medicine for health policy and the armed forces could nominate people to advise on the practicalities of war and defence.

It doesn't need to be said that such a Union would be a superpower the likes of which have never existed in the history of mankind. It's economic might would be extraordinary with a nominal GDP of $23.02 trillion, soaring above the $17.96 trillion of the EU, $17.69 trillion of the US or $9.4 trillion of China. It would have a population of 449 million, giving a GDP per capita of $51,270. This is in comparison to the $35,430 for the EU and $6,807 for China. Militarily we all co-operate already with organisations like the Five Eyes but with a united military we would be unquestionably dominant. We would never have to fear the growing might of authoritarian countries as we could be completely self sufficient if we chose to be.

Of course there are multiple problems with such a Union:

  • It would be difficult to reconcile the USA, a presidential republic with the Commonwealth parliamentary monarchies in a common political system. I would argue that by contributing representatives at the state rather than federal level we largely side-step this problem as it's irrelevant to Texas or Oregon whether or not Ontario, Wales or Queensland have a Queen or not. The Union would be based on existing structures as much as possible and would aim to absorb only what powers are absolutely required, everything else will be left alone. At any rate the EU is a combination of monarchies and republics and it doesn't seem to be a major factor in it's functioning. Of course, if the USA did not want to join such an organisation there would still be an argument for a similar organisation with the other countries I mentioned which would eliminate many (but not all) potential political problems.

  • There are still large economic differences between the countries. I can't really comment on this as I'm not educated in economics but I'd definitely say a common currency would be absolutely out of the question. In terms of development we're all reasonably equal, even the smallest economy in the bloc wouldn't really be comparable to say Germany and Romania but there's certainly a huge difference in terms of GDP between the USA and the rest of us. Then there's things like standardisation, Australia, Canada and New Zealand use the metric system while we use both and the Americans use traditional units. To be honest we'd probably all have to revert to American measures as their industry is too big and expensive to convert (which is why they never metricated in the first place) though this wouldn't be a major concern as long as we didn't have to drink US pints!

  • Even if we could convince the USA to participate they might just use it to more effectively dominate the rest of us. I personally don't think this is a concern. There's no reason British English, Australian English, Canadian English and New Zealand English would cease to be official in those areas so the Americanisation of English wouldn't be a worry. Culturally we influence America just as much as they influence us, just look how popular our music and television is over there. Economically the freer we are to trade with America the better.
The case for an Anglophone Union

As much as I would like to believe in such a union, realistically it is unlikely to succeed. There are only two real ways to approach it: true federalism or a loose confederation as you propose. The former option is too politically unpalatable, as most people don't want to give up their sense of nationality. The latter is destined for failure due to lack of integration and infighting, as happened with the US Articles of Confederation and as is currently happening with the EU.

Personally, I do think that the Anglosphere is culturally similar enough to work as a nation, but we're a long way away from convincing enough of our fellows to go along with it.

I propose a Union of countries that share a common language, have cultural similarities and ultimately a common origin.

Your plan would not work because such countries no longer exist in the West.

It might work in the East where countries like Tibet , Japan, and China still maintain a large degree of their cultural heritage.

Laptop user here. Any advice on standard cleaning practices?

I get really nervous about taking the casing off. The way the screws are positioned and (I guess) some plastic tabs or something. I'm convinced I'm going to destroy my machine.

As long as you're not stripping the screws you're fine. Look up your model of laptop and find a guide on taking it apart, usually the first result is a youtube video.

Easiest thing you can do is blow air into the vents using compressed air. You can also use the bristles of a toothbrush for any electronics as they don't generate an electric charge.
Step 1: Power off and unplug your machine before you clean it.
Dust is okay; but one of the worst things is moisture accumulating inside the chassis. Slime mold can (and will) actually grow inside if the conditions are right.
